prompt: Review the files under `fixture/` and make the production architecture decision for the notification fan-out pipeline. Write the decision to `docs/architecture.md`, including a components table and a concise explanation of the tradeoffs among all candidate options. The document must contain a fenced block whose info string is exactly `decision`; that block must contain JSON with exactly these keys: `chosen` (the option id), `options` (the array of option ids considered), `limits` (an object mapping each hard-limit name to {"limit": number, "value": number}, with one entry per hard limit in the inputs and the chosen option's computed value), and `monthly_cost_usd` (the chosen option's monthly cost computed from the price sheet). Use these exact `limits` keys: `throughput_msg_s`, `p99_delivery_seconds`, `monthly_budget_usd`, `payload_bytes`, `rpo_seconds`, and `rto_minutes`. Use option id `single-queue-pool` for the one managed queue with a consumer pool option, `topic-regional-queues` for the one topic with a queue in each service region option, and `stream-partitions` for the partitioned stream with independent delivery workers option, and list all three ids in `options`. Use the traffic schedule, service quotas, recovery objectives, and billing inputs together rather than relying on a single headline figure. Make the reported figures clear enough to audit against the source files. Keep the architecture practical for the stated peak and operational objectives.

checks.cmd: cp hidden/meta.json meta.json && mkdir -p fixture && cp -r hidden/_pristine/. fixture/ && ( [ -L solution ] || [ ! -e solution ] || mv solution .bench-agent-solution ) && ln -sfn . solution && node --require ./hidden/gate.js --test hidden/*.test.js

rubric.criterion: Explains why the selected design balances quota headroom, delivery latency, recovery targets, operational complexity, and cost better than the alternatives. Fail: picks on cost or keeps single-queue-pool, or sizes on the 2,500 msg/s sandbox quota or the 8 s p99. Partial: rejects single-queue-pool for throughput but does not weigh the two workable options on latency, recovery and cost. Pass: shows single-queue-pool tops out at 3,000 msg/s against the 6,000 msg/s peak (and extra workers do not raise the per-queue quota), notes topic-regional-queues (3 x 3,000 = 9,000 msg/s) and stream-partitions (8 x 1,000 = 8,000 msg/s) both clear the peak, weighs the chosen one on the 3-second p99, the 60-second RPO, the 15-minute RTO and the 4,500 USD budget, and says whether its capacity depends on how traffic spreads. (not code-checkable: Tests can recompute limits and cost but cannot judge whether the comparison is technically convincing or whether the tradeoff reasoning is complete.)

Presents a coherent set of components and responsibilities that could implement the selected fan-out design without contradicting the source assumptions. Fail: no components table, or components that contradict the limits (for example one queue carrying peak). Partial: a table exists but responsibilities overlap or the cost basis is unclear. Pass: the table gives each component one responsibility and an end-to-end path from ingress to delivery that stays within the 3,000 msg/s per-queue quota (not the sandbox 2,500), and the monthly cost uses the schedule of 2 peak hours at 6,000 msg/s plus 22 hours at 1,800 msg/s for 30 days. (not code-checkable: A script can find a table or decision block but cannot assess whether the components form a practical end-to-end architecture.)

The record rejects each option it did not choose for a reason taken from the fixture (a limit, a cost, a requirement or a measurement), and states the consequence of the chosen option the team must live with. Fail: names the winner only, or rejects options for generic reasons ("too complex", "not scalable") the fixture does not support. Partial: most rejected options get a fixture-based reason, but one is waved away or the cost of the chosen option is not stated. Pass: every rejected option has a reason quoted or computed from the fixture, the chosen option's main downside is stated, and the record says what would change the decision. (code cannot check this because tests check the chosen id and the numbers, not whether each rejection is grounded)

verdicts.note: The prompt references options.json by name for candidate enumeration but does not hint at the correct answer or a specific method.
All limits are clearly stated with units; the traffic schedule, service quotas, and pricing inputs have unambiguous numeric values and definitions.
The fixture provides all inputs but requires cross-file synthesis to discover that single-queue-pool fails the throughput constraint.
The task requires genuine multi-file analysis, limit calculation, and cost estimation; picking the cheapest option incorrectly fails the throughput check.
All required numbers (peak rate, quota, pricing, hours, multipliers) are present in the fixture files with clear definitions.

items.note: Prompt specifies option IDs and limit keys as naming conventions; no misleading hints about approach.
Fixture provides traffic schedule, quotas, objectives but not the decision; developer must evaluate tradeoffs.
Prompt states exact limit keys per edits.md fix; expertKey references throughput, latency, recovery calculations from fixture; rubric anchors on quota analysis.
Developer can evaluate three options against throughput, latency, recovery, cost objectives using provided data.

items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only
items.text: Says the topic design's 9,000 msg/s holds only if peak spreads across the three regions, because each regional queue has its own 3,000 msg/s quota, and that the packet gives no regional split (or that a region above 3,000 msg/s overflows). Also counts: the same point for stream partition keys. Weak: '9,000 is enough'. Do not require a numeric split.

weakAnswers: Picks single-queue-pool as the cheapest option without checking that its 3,000 msg/s capacity fails the 6,000 msg/s peak requirement.
Computes monthly cost by multiplying peak rate (6,000 msg/s) across all 720 hours instead of using the traffic schedule with 2 peak hours and 22 baseline hours per day.
Assumes adding workers to single-queue-pool increases throughput capacity, missing that the quota is per-queue and workers do not affect ingress limits.
Says the chosen option meets every objective without its own p99, RPO and RTO figures.

adjudication: Test the figure used, not the mention: an answer that sizes on the production figures and never names the superseded ones is correct; using a superseded figure in sizing fails the item it feeds.
Numbers within 1% of the key (rounding, 4,964.62 vs 4,965) are full credit; a figure with no working shown is Partial on an item that asks for working.
One mistake, one penalty: the same wrong figure in prose and in the decision block is one Partial, not two.
A limit equal to its bound meets it (150 MB/s against a 150 MB/s minimum, 60 s against 60 s); headroom is an expert point, never a fail.
Both topic-regional-queues and stream-partitions are correct; never fail an answer for picking one over the other when e6 is argued with figures.

payload_bytes: the packet makes the 2,048-byte contract the hard target (service-limits.md); an answer that reports the 4,096-byte broker maximum as the limit is Partial on the judge side, and the hidden test wants 2,048.
rto_minutes given in seconds with the unit stated is credited by the judge; the hidden test wants minutes.
A cost within 10% with one part missing (for example transfer) is Partial on e4.
